full_judgment:
17. The earliest case on this question appears to be that of Calcutta High Court, being the case of Shahebjada Faridun Shika Vs. Muhammad and others reported in 24 I.C. 802, in which Mukherjee and Neschareff JJ. were of the view that an order removing receiver was not an order under section 204 of the old Code of Civil Procedure (analogous to Order 40 Rule 1 C.P. Code) and as such was not appealable and in the case of Eastern Mortgage and Agency Co. Ltd. Vs. Premananda Saha and others reported in 20 C.W.N. 789 same case A.I.R. 1916 Calcutta 624 under the new code also it was held that no appeal lay from an order refusing to remove a receiver. This view of the Calcutta High Court appears to have been followed by the Madras High Court in the case of Ramaswarai Naidu and others Vs. Avvalu Naidu, reported in A.I.R. 1924 Madras 614 same case 78 Indian case 625. The Calcutta High Court, appears, however, to have shed new light on this question in the case of Sripati Dutta Vs. Bibhuti Bhusan Dutta, reported in A.I.R. 1926 Cal. 593, same case ILR 53 Cal. 319 same case 92 I.C. 940. where it has been laid down that an order dismissing an application for removal of a receiver may be construed to be an order under Order 40 rule 1 C.P. Code and as such it is appealable. It has been pointed out it the said case that when a person is authorized to do an act it is necessarily implied, according to section 16 of General Clauses Act that he is empowered to under the act and the power to appoint includes the power to remove or dismiss. The Court empowered to appoint a receiver under clause (a) of rule 1 of Order 40 of the Code, it has the necessary power to remove the receiver under the provision of the Code, read with section 16 of the General Clauses Act, and so an order of removal of receiver is necessarily an order under rule (1) of Order 40., and as such it is appealable under Order 43 rule 1(s) of the Code.  The Allahabad High Court however dissented from the above view of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Anthony Ullyssess John and others Vs. Agra United Mills Ltd. and another reported in A.I.R. 1931 Allahabad 72, same case 134 IC. 454. The High Court of Rangoon, however, has followed the later Calcutta view reported in A.I.R. 1926 Calcutta 593, in preference to that propounded in the earlier case reported in A T.R. 1916 Calcutta 824 in the case of Abdul Kader VS. R. M. P. Chattyar Film in A.I.R. 1938 Ran. 387 same case 178 I.C. 924 and held that an order refusing to remove a receiver is appealable. The Allahahad High Court appears to have revised its earlier view in the case of Allahabad Bank Ltd. Vs. Maharaj Kishore Khanna and others, in A.I.R. 1945 All 371 in which it dissented from the view expressed in A.I.R. 1931 All 72 and followed that of the Calcutta High Court, as expressed in A.I.R. 1926 Calcutta 593. The Patna High Court, in the case of Surendra Nath Sarkar Vs. Nagar Chand Goenka and another reported in A.I.R. 1947 Pat. 418 same case 25 Patna 779 made a distinction between an order removing a receiver and an order refusing to remove a receiver. Fazl Ali J (as he then was) in delivering the judgment the Court has held, following 20 C.W.N. 789, in A.I.R. 1924 Madras 614 and A.I.R. 1931 All 72, that although an order removing a receiver may be deemed to be an order under Rule 1 of Order 40, but an order refusing to remove a receiver cannot be deemed to be an order under the said provision, and as such it is not appealable. This judicial controversy was sought to be set at rest, so far as the courts in Indian jurisdiction were concerned, by the Federal Court of India in the case of Kutoor Vengayil Rayarappan Nayanar Vs. Rutoor Vengayil Valla Madhavi Amma and others, reported in A.I.R. 1950 F. C. 140, in which the view of the Calcutta High Court as expressed in A.I.R. 1926 'Calcutta 593 was approved and those expressed in A.I.R. 1916 Calcutta 824, 1924 a Mad. 614 and 1931 All 72 were disapproved. Mahajan J in delivering the judgment of the Federal Court observed as follows : 

 The High Court of Travancore-Cochin in Indian jurisdiction without noticing the aforesaid Federal Court decision followed the view of the Patna High Court as expressed in A. I. R. 1947 Patna 418 in the case or Kochu Kumari Vs. Krishnan Janardhanan, Reported in, A.I.R. 1952 Travancore-Cochin 248 on the question of appeal ability of an order of refusal to remove receiver but the position was set right by the same High Court in a subsequent decision in the case of Velayudhan Narayanan Vs. Matheran Narayani and others, reported In A.I.R. 1955 Travancore-Cochin 163 in which the view expressed in A.I.R. 1950 (F. C.) 140 was followed.
